summary: Specifies how an ALTO client embedded in a resource consumer can discover ALTO servers before asking for guidance.

eli5.summary: Before you can ask a guide for directions, you first need to find where the guide is. This explains how.

subtitle: How an ALTO client finds its server using a domain name from DHCP or local settings, then a DNS U-NAPTR lookup.

tldr.problem: An ALTO client cannot ask for guidance on choosing among candidate hosts until it knows where an ALTO server is.
tldr.mechanism: The client first gets a domain name from local configuration or DHCP, then does a U-NAPTR lookup with the ALTO service tag to obtain the HTTP or HTTPS URI of the server's Information Resource Directory.
tldr.outcome: It covers only discovery started by a resource consumer with an embedded ALTO client. Third-party discovery is a different approach left to another document.

today: RFC 7286 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It supports the ALTO protocol defined in RFC 7285.

sections.title: The Discovery Problem
sections.content:
Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) gives guidance to applications that must choose one or several hosts from a set of candidates able to provide a resource. ALTO is a client-server protocol, so a client first has to discover one or more ALTO servers that can advise it.

This RFC specifies resource-consumer-initiated discovery, usable when the ALTO client is embedded in the resource consumer. A different approach, third-party discovery, is addressed in another document. The ALTO protocol (RFC 7285) expects discovery to yield the HTTP or HTTPS URI of the server's Information Resource Directory (IRD), which describes the capabilities and services of that server.
sections.eli5: An ALTO server is like a helpful guide. Before asking it anything, your program has to learn where the guide lives.

sections.title: Step 1: Getting a Domain Name
sections.content:
Discovery runs in two steps, and it is performed for every address family on every interface the application considers. Step 1 gets one DNS domain name per interface and address family. The procedure first checks for a locally configured name, and only then asks DHCP. If neither gives a name, the procedure fails with an appropriate error code.

Local configuration lets a user enter a name, for example my-alternative-alto-provider.example.org. This is useful where no DHCP server exists or when the user wants an ALTO service not run by the network operator. Implementations MAY allow a name per address family on each interface and SHOULD allow a default name.

DHCP is the primary means. For IPv6 the procedure MUST try option 57 (OPTION_V6_ACCESS_DOMAIN); if absent it fails for that interface. For IPv4 it MUST try option 213 (OPTION_V4_ACCESS_DOMAIN) and SHOULD then try option 15 (Domain Name). A result such as example.net goes to step 2. A reverse (PTR) lookup on the client's address is not recommended because of NAT.
sections.eli5: First the program finds the name of its network, either because you typed it in or because the network told it. If it finds nothing, it gives up.

sections.title: Step 2: U-NAPTR Resolution
sections.content:
Each domain name is used as the application-unique string in a U-NAPTR lookup (RFC 4848) with the Application Service Tag ALTO and the Application Protocol Tag http or https. The result is one or more URIs for the server's IRD, and may be any valid HTTP(S) URI. Only these two schemes are defined because the ALTO protocol uses only them.

In the RFC's example, two records map example.net to https://alto1.example.net/ird and https://alto2.example.net/ird, with the first preferred through its lower order value. Further DNS lookups may be needed to find the server's IP addresses.

If no ALTO-specific U-NAPTR records are found, discovery fails for that domain name, interface and IP version. Before retrying a failed lookup, a client MUST wait a period suited to the error, such as NXDOMAIN or timeout.
sections.eli5: The program looks the network name up in a special phone book that lists ALTO guides, and gets back the web address of one or two of them.

sections.title: Deployment Issues
sections.content:
Some home gateways do not pass unknown DHCP options through, which effectively removes the option. Others substitute their own domain name, such as .local, for the operator's, and that name is generally unusable for discovery unless the gateway's DNS server answers the NAPTR lookup correctly, for example with split horizon DNS.

Multihoming and mobility complicate things. A single default name in local configuration finds one set of servers regardless of interface, which can give poor results on mobile hosts. DHCP can find different servers per interface and address family, and a client SHOULD query the servers discovered for the interface and family it is using. A change of IP address invalidates the result, so discovery must be re-run without relying on earlier information. Choosing among interfaces or comparing answers from different servers is out of scope.

With VPNs there is usually no DHCP, so the user has to enter a domain name that corresponds to the VPN concentrator rather than the user's current location.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the home router garbles the message, or you move to a new network. Then the program has to look for the guide all over again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC treats four scenarios. The most serious is integrity of the discovered URI: a wrong server might give no guidance, or suboptimal or forged information, and a hostile one could threaten privacy. Local configuration, DHCP and DNS are each an attack vector. DHCP is prone to forged replies and best current practices should be followed. DNSSEC can limit tampering with the U-NAPTR records. If TLS protects ALTO, only the host part of the HTTPS URI is authenticated, so the DNS mapping must be secured as well.

For availability, if no server can be found applications must decide without ALTO guidance, and operators should protect their DHCP, DNS and ALTO servers against denial of service.

For confidentiality of the server's URI and privacy for clients, no protection is provided because the RFC says neither has been identified as a relevant threat; the server URI has been considered public information. If a new use case needs it, the procedure must be re-evaluated.
sections.eli5: If a trickster slips you a fake address for the guide, you could get bad directions. Locking down the network name lookups helps prevent that.
